lesson.title: Where the Wave Starts: Understanding Phase Angle
lesson.summary: Phase angle is the extra angle added inside a sinusoid's argument that shifts where the waveform sits at time zero, without changing its shape, amplitude, or frequency.
lesson.body:
A general sinusoidal voltage is written as v(t) = Vm sin(omega t + theta), where Vm is the peak amplitude, omega is the angular frequency you just met, and theta is the phase angle. The phase angle does not change how tall the wave is or how fast it oscillates, it only changes where the wave happens to be along its cycle at the instant t = 0. Think of omega t as a clock hand sweeping around a circle at a steady rate. The phase angle theta is simply the starting position of that hand before the sweep begins. A positive theta starts the hand further along the circle, meaning the waveform reaches its peak earlier than a plain sin(omega t) reference would.

This matters because in real circuits, voltage and current waveforms rarely cross zero at exactly the same instant, even though they share the same frequency. Resistors keep voltage and current perfectly aligned, but capacitors and inductors introduce a delay between the two because of how they store and release energy. Describing that delay requires a number, and phase angle, measured in degrees or radians, is that number. A capacitor's current leads its voltage, and an inductor's current lags its voltage, and both relationships are expressed as differences in phase angle between the two waveforms.

Worked example: suppose a signal generator outputs v(t) = 100 sin(377t + 30 degrees) volts, where 377 rad/s corresponds to a 60 Hz signal as found earlier. To find the instantaneous voltage at t = 0, substitute directly: v(0) = 100 sin(0 + 30 degrees) = 100 sin(30 degrees). Since sin(30 degrees) equals 0.5 exactly, v(0) = 100 times 0.5 = 50 volts. Compare that to a reference wave with no phase angle, v_ref(t) = 100 sin(377t), which gives v_ref(0) = 100 sin(0 degrees) = 0 volts. The phase angle of 30 degrees accounts for the entire difference: the phase shifted wave has already risen to 50 volts by the time the reference wave is still sitting at zero.

Phase angle is always measured relative to some chosen reference, most often either time zero or another waveform of the same frequency. By convention, a pure sine with no added angle, sin(omega t), is taken to have a phase angle of zero, and every other waveform of the same frequency is described relative to it. Degrees and radians are both used in practice, and it is worth being fluent converting between them: 30 degrees equals pi/6 radians, since 180 degrees equals pi radians exactly, and pi/6 is approximately 0.5236 radians.

A subtlety worth flagging is that phase angle only has meaning when comparing signals of the same frequency. Two waveforms at different frequencies drift relative to each other constantly, so their relative phase angle is not a fixed number, it changes with every instant that passes. This is exactly the setup you need to understand phase shift, which describes the phase angle difference between two related waveforms of identical frequency.
